title: Investors poured over $13 billion into just 56 AI startups in the first four months of 2021 alone – VCs and CEOs explain why everyone is trying to cash in
text:
- There have been 56 "mega-rounds" or $100 million or more in the AI sector so far this year.
- VCs and CEOs say big bets show AI has been supercharged by COVID-19 as companies rapidly adopt it.
- AI is where search engines, social media, and customer relationship management were in past eras.
- See more stories on Insider's business page.
Welcome to the era of artificial intelligence "mega-rounds," where investors write checks to AI startups bigger than your average lottery jackpot.
So far this year, venture capital firms have invested in artificial intelligence startups with 56 rounds of $100 million or more, according to investor database PitchBook. That's more mega-rounds than there were by this time in the previous five years, combined.
In those mega-rounds alone – just the tip of the iceberg of AI investing so far this year – investors gave startups a staggering $13.8 billion. It's a huge milestone for a sector once seen as cool and interesting, but not mature enough for big-time investment. An economy struggling to get up to speed after COVID-19 is embracing AI as never before, leaders of the sector say. And investors don't want to miss out.
CEOs, investors and analysts say the big rounds are proof that AI's time has come – not in theory, or as the next shiny object to dazzle the imagination – but as a reality for companies big and small. AI is where search engines were in 2005, where social media was in 2010, and where customer relationship management was in 2015, these insiders say. It is simply changing everything.
Insiders expect a few companies will rise to be the next batch of trillion-dollar companies, following in the footsteps of Apple, Microsoft, or Amazon before them. But there will be more big companies in AI creating a new world, and the investors believe that writing sizable checks now will create more and bigger payoffs.
"From the investor's point of view, big bets are coming for the companies that are rising to seize opportunities," investor Lip-Bu Tan of SoftBank told Insider.
Ali Ghodsi, the CEO of Databricks, raised the biggest AI round of all so far in 2021, announcing a $1 billion in February. And his firm did it without even showing investors a slide deck of what it plans to do with the money.
"In January we said, 'Let's go fund-raise. My CFO said, 'They're pinging me already. I don't think we'll need a pitch deck.' I thought he was crazy," Ghodsi told Insider. "We argued about it. It took us rounds A, B, C, D, E, and F to raise our first billion. In one week he got another billion, just like that. It was insane."
The $1 billion Series G round led by Franklin Templeton Investments put the company's pre-money valuation at $27 billion. You would need some kind of AI algorithm to keep track of all the investors, which include Microsoft, Amazon Web Services, Salesforce Ventures, Dragoneer Investment and 17 others.
Ghodsi said Databricks, a San Francisco startup of 1,700 that helps companies process data with AI tools, passed on an investor who wanted to put $750 million into the round, because others had already committed and the round was getting too large. "They don't want to miss out. I'm not even sure they have time to do due diligence."
With all that cash in a few pockets and a crowded field of startups, acquisitions are inevitable, Ghodsi believes – and Databricks plans to pursue some. "Consolidation will happen. With this much capital, it's bound to happen."
The COVID-19 pandemic has contributed to a sudden burst of innovation as companies emerge from quarantine, Ghodsi believes. "People's mindsets have changed. For a year we woke up every day and did the same thing. Now vaccines have been created, with the help of AI. So maybe it's possible to do many things that have held society back."
'From the investor's point of view, big bets are coming'
SoftBank's Tan agrees that COVID-19 research has supercharged what was already a powerhouse AI sector. "AI has become the great enabler of innovation," he told Insider. "There has been a data explosion, but then the question arose of how companies were going to use it. You saw how with healthcare, new drug discovery, and COVID-19."
Tan took part in SamaNova's $650 million round earlier this month in his role as external board director of SoftBank, and has been chairman of the board of the startup since 2018 when Walden International and GV led the company's Series A. SoftBank has invested in AI behemoths Nvidia, TikTik-owner Bytedance and the automated car company Cruise.
Rodrigo Liang, CEO of SambaNova, a chipmaker specializing in AI hardware that has seen its valuation skyrocket to $5.1 billion, told Insider that amid COVID-19, research companies like his "became a showcase of what technology can do in the face of some really hard problems." Now, he believes companies coming out of the pandemic are "looking aggressively to catch up" and automation based on AI will play a key role.
"AI could be as big of an innovation as the internet was," Liang said. "It's going to be a force everyone has to materialize for their companies to be competitive."
SambaNova will also look to make acquisitions with its windfall of cash, which brings its total venture capital raised to $1.1 billion. The series D round also included new investors Temasek and GIC, plus existing backers including funds and accounts managed by BlackRock, Intel Capital, GV (formerly Google Ventures), Walden International and WRVI.
Alex Ferrara, a partner at Bessemer Venture Partners, is an investor in BigID, which uses AI and machine learning to help companies track and use their data, and KHealth, which helps patients get medical information and healthcare. Companies need help wrangling data, he told Insider, providing a massive opportunity for AI as COVID-19 gradually releases its grip on the American economy.
"Big banks are reading headcount and seeing they have to do more with less. That means automation." That automation will include tackling the huge data sets companies have collected over the past several years. "Some don't even know where their data is stored" in cloud servers, he said. "They need a tool" such as those BigID provides, he said.
Alex Wang, the CEO of Scale AI, which prepares raw data for processing at scale, just reeled in a $325 million Series E round from lead investors led by Dragoneer Investment Group, Greenoaks Capital Partners, and Tiger Global Management to take his company's valuation "north of a billion dollars." His San Francisco startup has hired 100 people he's never met in person during the COVID-19 remote-work era as it works with big customers including PayPal, Toyota, and Etsy.
Wang told Insider that AI has gotten real for many in just the past few months. "What used to seem like a leap of faith has become critical for companies."
For that reason, he said, "investors are going all-in."

title: Precipice Edginess When A Self-Driving Car Drives Down A Super-Steep Slope Like These Top Ten U.S. Vertical-Drop Streets
text:
Have you ever been driving and found yourself at the top edge of a really steep incline?
I’m talking about a monster of a dizzying slope.
A gradient of tremendous and heart-pounding fear-inducing scope can be altogether unsettling. The downward tilt is seemingly equal to being on a roller coaster at the moment that you are looking below you and praying that things hold together, and you’ll live through the experience.
Of course, when on an active roadway in the real-world, the qualms about being on a steep incline are more pressing than a joyous ride on a roller coaster, especially since you are at the wheel of the car and ultimately responsible for any life-or-death consequences that might arise. You are the captain of the ship. The car is at the crest of a tsunami-sized wave and you don’t know for sure that the craft won’t be crumpled as it descends the mighty swell.
When caught in such a dire predicament, you likely are pressing your face forward toward the front windshield of your car, hoping to somehow peek over the hood and manage to see what is on the other side of this monstrous hill you are on. The thing is, you probably cannot see the road at all due to your car being pitched somewhat upward at the crest, and all that exists beyond your vision is the vast skyline.
This means that you cannot directly see the road.
For all you know, your car is going to gingerly pass over this toppling crest and then shockingly end-up falling into an endless abyss. You don’t believe in your heart of hearts that such an outcome is possible. There is supposed to be a roadway ahead, and you are assuming that there must be since otherwise, you would have to abandon all hope.
So, you tease forward by giving your car just a slight inch of pressure on the accelerator pedal. The vehicle crawls over the crest like those old war serials that showcased military tanks trying to get over rows of blocking hedges. For a few heart-stopping moments, your car is seemingly in nowhere land as it comes off the upward slope and pitches downward.
Then, with a gasp of relief, you realize that there is indeed a road and your tires are thankfully still engaged with the surface of the street. You can see the roadway once again!
The problem now becomes one of quickly scanning the driving scene ahead of you. Are there any parked cars that are threatening to be in the way as you come down this steep incline? Are pedestrians anywhere in the street or nearby to the roadway? Is there any traffic coming up the incline that might be dangerously close to your car as you make your way downward?
All of those factors would normally be scanned for and be detected long in-advance when driving on a relatively flat and altogether horizontal roadway. This vertical drop makes for some dicey driving. You don’t know exactly what you will confront after successfully navigating the crest. You have just a few split seconds to rapidly examine the road conditions ahead and make any nearly instantaneous adjustments to your steering, your braking, and your acceleration, hoping to contend with whatever exists on the other side of this cliffhanging experience.
Maybe you don’t live in an area that has roads of this nature. If so, perhaps be thankful you don’t need to contend with them, else your heart might give out. Or, you might readily get into a car wreck, which can happen easily in these crazy gradient circumstances.
Generally, many localities put up warning signs for any streets that might involve a 7% or greater grade (the higher the number, the greater the degree of tilt). In technical terms, the grade of a road is its vertical location with respect to the ground surface, measured typically via the tangent of the angle of that surface to the horizontal. In layman’s language, if your breath is taken away by the slope or pitch, the road is probably a darned steep one.
Various roadway infrastructure reporting suggests that the following list constitutes the Top 10 steepest inclines in the United States for drivable roadways that are publicly available for driving on (though, there is plenty of argument and debate over such lists):
- 45% gradient in Hawaii (Waipio Rd. in Honokaa)
- 37% gradient in Pennsylvania (Canton Ave. in Pittsburgh)
- 33% gradient in California (Eldred St. in Los Angeles)
- 33% gradient in California (28th St. in Los Angeles)
- 32% gradient in California (Baxter St. in Los Angeles)
- 32% gradient in California (Fargo St. in Los Angeles)
- 32% gradient in California (Maria Ave. in Spring Valley)
- 32% gradient in Pennsylvania (Dornbush St. in Pittsburgh)
- 32% gradient in California (22nd St. in San Francisco)
- 32% gradient in California (Filbert St. in San Francisco)
Those are assuredly whoppers, regardless of whether they belong on a Top 10 list or not.
Truth be told, any such steep street is a danger to society, sorry to say.
Despite the thrill or excitement involved in traversing such a road, you have to take into account the fact that these steep streets are patently hazardous for all concerned parties. The driver is blindly proceeding ahead. There might be everyday pedestrians in the street and they’ll get run down. There might be a car coming up the hill and you’ll ram head-to-head into the vehicle. You might sideswipe parked cars that have been (riskily) parked on the sloping street and thus lose total control of your vehicle. And so on.
Technically, these are referred to as terrain slope-induced driving problems.
As a human driver, some take all this in stride. People that drive down these roads on a daily basis might vehemently swear that they’ve never encountered any difficulties. To them, the massive descent is no different than driving on the flats of a pancaked desert.
Good for them, but this doesn’t provide proof of safety. They have managed to somehow exploit their lucky rabbits’ foot and never had any issues arise on the slope. One might argue they are living on borrowed time.
There is also the matter of drivers that encounter the steep slope for the first time. Those first-timers are not only faced with the challenges of driving the steepness in a safe manner, but they might also react adversely to the situation and become panicked in their drivable ways. In essence, the human reaction to the predicament could produce an untoward outcome, regardless of whether by default alone a calamity might have laid in wait.
For those of you that are movie buffs, you undoubtedly have watched the famous car chase scene by Steve McQueen in the action-thriller movie Bullitt. He drives a Ford Mustang GT Fastback through the hilly streets of San Francisco while chasing after the villains in a Dodge Charger. If you want to virtually get a palpable sense of what it is like to drive down steep slopes, make sure to watch the video posting of this iconic car chase. Be prepared for a bit of vertigo and being on the edge of your seat.
Why all this discussion about driving down steeply sloped streets?
Consider that the future of cars entails the advent of self-driving cars (for my ongoing coverage see the link here). AI-based true self-driving cars will drive autonomously, meaning that the AI is doing all of the driving. There is no human involvement and the AI is utterly in-charge of the driving controls.
Here is today’s intriguing question: When a true self-driving car comes upon the precipice of a really steep street, how good will it do at coping with such a driving dilemma?
Let’s unpack the matter and see.
Understanding The Levels Of Self-Driving Cars
As a clarification, true self-driving cars are ones that the AI drives the car entirely on its own and there isn’t any human assistance during the driving task.
These driverless vehicles are considered Level 4 and Level 5 (see my explanation at this link here), while a car that requires a human driver to co-share the driving effort is usually considered at Level 2 or Level 3. The cars that co-share the driving task are described as being semi-autonomous, and typically contain a variety of automated add-on’s that are referred to as ADAS (Advanced Driver-Assistance Systems).
There is not yet a true self-driving car at Level 5, which we don’t yet even know if this will be possible to achieve, and nor how long it will take to get there.
Meanwhile, the Level 4 efforts are gradually trying to get some traction by undergoing very narrow and selective public roadway trials, though there is controversy over whether this testing should be allowed per se (we are all life-or-death guinea pigs in an experiment taking place on our highways and byways, some contend, see my coverage at this link here).
Since semi-autonomous cars require a human driver, the adoption of those types of cars won’t be markedly different than driving conventional vehicles, so there’s not much new per se to cover about them on this topic (though, as you’ll see in a moment, the points next made are generally applicable).
For semi-autonomous cars, it is important that the public needs to be forewarned about a disturbing aspect that’s been arising lately, namely that despite those human drivers that keep posting videos of themselves falling asleep at the wheel of a Level 2 or Level 3 car, we all need to avoid being misled into believing that the driver can take away their attention from the driving task while driving a semi-autonomous car.
You are the responsible party for the driving actions of the vehicle, regardless of how much automation might be tossed into a Level 2 or Level 3.
Self-Driving Cars And Daredevil Gradients
For Level 4 and Level 5 true self-driving vehicles, there won’t be a human driver involved in the driving task.
All occupants will be passengers.
The AI is doing the driving.
One aspect to immediately discuss entails the fact that today’s AI is not sentient. In other words, the AI is altogether a collective of computer-based programming and algorithms, and most assuredly not able to reason in the same manner that humans can. For example, current AI lacks any semblance of common sense and nor has any kind of common-sense reasoning (for further background, see the link here).
This is important to keep in mind when considering how a self-driving car will deal with a steep slope and a potentially daredevil descent. There isn’t any semblance of human judgment, human intuition, or similar human-specific qualities. Of course, the other side of that coin can be argued as doing away with the emotional reactions that can arise when confronting a dicey driving situation such as a steep decline.
In any case, let’s start at the beginning.
A self-driving car contains a slew of sensors to aid in detecting the outside world. The typical sensor suite includes video cameras, radar, LIDAR, ultrasonic units, and the like. These electronic devices are intended to be the veritable eyes and ears of the self-driving car. Mounted on various positions of the self-driving car, these sensors are continually collecting data about whatever is detectable in the surrounding driving scene.
The AI driving system then mathematically examines the sensory data and tries to figure out what the driving scene consists of. Crucial fundamentals such as where the drivable roadway surface exists have to be calculated and ferreted out. Humans take for granted that they can see the road and divine that the road is drivable. All of that has to be painstakingly computed by the AI driving system.
One aspect that outsiders of the self-driving industry do not take into account is the inherent limitations of those sensors. Different types of sensors are detecting the surroundings in differing ways. Some types of sensors do better in certain kinds of conditions, such as whether it is sunny versus cloudy, dry versus raining, etc. Also, various sensors have key differences in terms of how far away they can detect objects. And so on.
Another key consideration is where the sensors are mounted.
Generally, the higher up the sensor is placed, the more likely the sensor will be unobstructed and be able to glean a wider expanse. If you have a sensor on the lower bumper of the car, the odds are that it can only do detection closer to the ground. Meanwhile, a sensor sitting atop the roof of the car is bound to have a more pronounced detection capacity (these are generalizations and dependent upon the nature of the sensors being used).
Okay, this sets the stage for the saga of arriving at a street that has a steep decline.
The self-driving car is cruising along and comes to the precipice of the sloped street. In many ways, the AI driving system is going to be confounded akin to how a human is confounded (do not though anthropomorphize the AI, as stated, it is not sentient). The odds are that the sensors will not readily be able to detect the road that lies ahead.
Assuming that the sensors are statically fixed in place on the vehicle, they will be aiming at a somewhat upward angle when the self-driving car reaches the crest. This limits their facility of detecting what is over-the-hill and down along the downward sloping street. In short, a significant aspect of the terrain slope-induced driving problem for self-driving cars is that the forward visibility is severely limited in settings such as a high gradient steeply sloped downward pitched street.
Humans take for granted that the road will continue. They make this assumption because they believe that other humans would have made sure the road continues (well, this applies in cities and is not necessarily the case for off-road driving). Furthermore, one would assume that unless a sign or warning signal is posted to alert you about some disaster waiting ahead, you are relatively safe to proceed.
In that same manner of logic, a self-driving car generally is programmed to make the same set of assumptions.
Note that this implies the self-driving car ought to be first detecting whether there are any posted warnings. Thus, a vital aspect of the AI driving system involves scanning the area while at the top of the crest, attempting to discover any signage or indication that perhaps the road ahead is not traversable.
You might be thinking that this is somewhat unnecessary since the self-driving car would certainly be armed with digitized maps and have GPS. In that case, there is no need to presumably be looking around for signage. Instead, merely consult the map. If the map indicates the road continues ahead, you are good to proceed. Case closed.
Well, maybe, maybe not.
First, you are making quite a big bet with the lives of all parties involved, as based solely on a map. The reality at the driving scene can oftentimes differ from a prior digitized map. Perhaps the map was updated a month ago. Meanwhile, there was roadwork done and just beyond the crest, there is a mighty pothole, waiting to ensnare cars that come down that street.
The use of a map is undoubtedly vital and an important element, but a map alone is not how anyone or anything should be driving a car. It is a reasonable expectation that the AI driving system ought to be using all of its sensors to try and figure out what the real-time situation consists of, in addition to using any available digitized maps.
Besides scanning for warning signs, another factor would be the status of other cars.
For example, suppose a car that was being human-driven was ahead of the self-driving car, reaching the summit first. Imagine that the human-driven car reaches the crest, comes to a halt, and then makes a U-turn. If you were driving in the car that was behind that turning around the car, what would you think? Most cautious drivers would think that maybe this other driver has determined that something ahead is amiss. Of course, that driver might simply be “a chicken” in that they don’t want to tempt fate by going down the gradient, or it could be that they saw something that alerted them to avoid a potential catastrophe.
One would also expect that the AI driving system will drive slowly, cautiously, and not try to breeze over the crest. Human drivers love to drive fast and especially on a hill that has steep slopes. Perhaps these daredevils get a rush or envision themselves acting like Steve McQueen. In any case, it is reasonable to expect that the AI driving system should not proceed brazenly and instead be soberly measured in how it approaches the setting.
That being said, there is a consequent danger that nearby human-driven cars will react adversely if they get stuck behind a self-driving car that seems to be inching along in such circumstances. This might prompt human drivers into veering around the snail-paced self-driving car. The end result could be quite dangerous for all concerned. Your first impulse is to assert that this is a problem associated with the human drivers and not the “fault” of the AI driving system. That seems like a satisfying reply, but it lacks real-world value and we need to ensure that self-driving cars can mix ably with human-driven traffic too (see my discussion at this link here).
After the crest, the AI driving system will need to quickly scan the road ahead, having (safely, one hopes) gone over the crest and now aiming downward on the steep slope. The sensors will once again have a viable chance of being able to discern what the roadway status is. This includes examining the sensory data to figure out where the roadway is, where pedestrians are, where parked cars are, and the rest.
If a self-driving car has previously driven that route, there can be a kind of templated expectation of what the upcoming driving scene is going to be like. This reduces the computational workload in the manner that the AI driving system only needs to update an expected scene, rather than render one from scratch.
An advantage of self-driving cars is that if even one self-driving car of a given fleet has ridden down a particular street, this, in theory, can be applied to the other self-driving cars in the fleet (using OTA, Over-The-Air electronic updating capabilities).
Conclusion
To help the AI driving system, other anticipated innovations are coming down the pike (whoa, that was a bit of a pun).
There are efforts underway to provide a paired drone with self-driving cars (see my coverage at this link here).
Essentially, a self-driving car would have a drone that sits atop the vehicle or maybe in a compartment on the trunk and can be launched into the air when so needed. The drone could fly ahead and look down upon the steep road, providing sensory data electronically to the vehicle and thus allow the self-driving car to readily be aware of what lies ahead.
Another upcoming innovation is the use of V2V (vehicle-to-vehicle) electronic communication.
This allows a self-driving car to broadcast an electronic message to other nearby self-driving cars. For example, if debris is sitting in the middle of a road, a self-driving car that detects the debris might emit a warning electronically to other self-driving cars that are within the same vicinity. Similarly, a self-driving car that goes down the steep slope can be transmitting V2V and inform other self-driving cars nearing the top crest about what to expect on the road below.
As much as possible, the hope is that the makers of self-driving cars will be on their toes and finding ways to reduce the risks of driving down those wildly steep avenues. Rather than passengers having to hold their breaths and make a leap of blind faith that the AI driving system has been well-devised, we are all likely only going to accept self-driving cars on our public roadways if they can manage to deal with all types of driving quandaries.
Think about this the next time you are in a human-driven car, and you are watching the face of the driver as they either tense-up when approaching a steep slope, or they get that devil-may-care look and decide to floor it for a car-rocking bone-jarring high-risk reckless drive on a slope meant for seasoned skiers in the snow-capped Alps.

title: Council Post: 2021's Top Six Emerging Industries To Invest In
text:
Kevin Leyes is the Chairman of Leyes Enterprises and the CEO of Leyes Media, an SMM and PR agency, and Team Leyes, an urban jewelry company.
In 2012, a video game developer named John Ratcliff got a bitcoin as a gift; it was worth $13 at the time. When he saw the value of bitcoin rising, he invested $15,000 in 150 bitcoins, each worth $100, back in 2013. In January, we saw Bitcoin reach $40,000 per coin. For Ratcliff, understanding where to invest has allowed him to build a $1.4 million house. He also recently put down a large payment for his new Tesla Roadster by selling just six of his bitcoins.
Ratcliff and others like him have seen huge profits because they saw early on that cryptocurrency was an emerging industry. They recognized its huge potential and are now cashing in. For many, this is the goal. That leaves us wondering where to invest. What industries are emerging today?
What Is An Emerging Industry?
According to Investopedia, “An emerging industry is a group of companies in a line of business formed around a new product or idea that is in the early stages of development.” These companies often come about as one technology takes over another, older technology. It’s important to note that stocks of companies in emerging industries can be volatile. That means that investing in these companies is risky. However, as John Ratcliff’s story and so many like it have proven, great risk can bring great reward.
Where To Invest Your Money In 2021: Six Emerging Industries
1. Artificial Intelligence
We’ve already seen artificial intelligence (AI) spreading into many areas of society and business operations. This trend will continue as artificial intelligence is continually developed and optimized to help in more ways, making it flexible and adaptable to various industries. AI has already become a part of the automotive industry with self-driving cars and the healthcare industry with virtual doctor visits. AI is here to stay, and it's becoming more and more ingrained into our everyday lives.
2. Virtual Reality
While virtual reality (VR) is a natural progression for the (already huge) video game industry, its adaptability shows its staying power. As Forbes reports, Covid-19 has sped up the need for digital collaboration. We’re seeing augmented and virtual reality integrated into the financial, entertainment, transportation, retail, healthcare and security sectors via their business applications. We’re also seeing VR push into government and academia, cementing virtual reality as more than a trend.
3. Renewable And Alternative Energy
Although renewable energy isn’t a new idea, it’s finally gaining more traction. We’ve seen the demand for electricity fall in 2020. Meanwhile, the demand for renewable energy has exceeded that of coal more than ever before (153 days in 2020 versus 39 in 2019.) With the U.S. rejoining the Paris Climate Accord and planning to invest $2 trillion in clean energy, we should see this industry accelerating in 2021.
4. Big Data Analytics
Big data analytics reviews large amounts of data, looking for hidden correlations and patterns. With new technology that can analyze big data and get answers in minutes, companies will be able to move more quickly than ever before. The result? Cost reduction, faster and more informed decision-making, and new products based on consumer feedback. All of these things mean more money for companies that use this technology.
5. Cybersecurity
As technology grows and changes, our cybersecurity needs will, as well. It will be more important than ever to protect our information. We can expect to see cybersecurity technology develop and change to meet new needs — including utilizing AI in new solutions. The cybersecurity market is expected to grow from $165.78 billion in 2021 to $366.10 billion by 2028.
6. Cloud Computing
Cloud computing as an industry is becoming increasingly standardized and compatible. Hosted private, hosted on-premises and public cloud infrastructure are allowing data streams to be much more mobile and workloads more portable. With this shift, we’re now seeing cloud computing supporting more processes, apps and services. The cloud computing market is projected to hit $760.98 billion by 2027.
Closing Thoughts
Investing in stocks in an emerging market can be life-changing. Emerging markets are very volatile, so it’s incredibly important to research before investing. You need to ensure that not only the industry but also the company you’re investing in has staying power; this will make all the difference. Knowing where to invest your money all comes down to research. From AI to cloud computing to cybersecurity, it’s clear that technology will rule future industries. Where will you invest first?

title: Council Post: IT Infrastructure Management: It Should Be Simple
text:
Field CTO for the Americas at Infinidat.
Simplicity is a path to improved productivity, but it is a road less traveled for far too many IT-related companies. Over the years, tech companies have been notorious for giving their users ever-increasing complexity instead of incrementally greater simplicity. In this decade of user experience, complexity will not be tolerated the way it has in the past. And this applies to the data storage industry as much as any other area of the IT field.
Complexity raises the risk of human error, wastes people’s time and prevents users from focusing on their other priorities. Technology should enable business operational efficiency, continuity and growth, not keep staff busy for the sake of being busy.
Even something as common as a physical storage hardware upgrade to an existing system introduces unnecessary complexity and can be avoided with more modern seamless approaches when adding capacity.
If you have fewer things that require management, you have more time to devote to more important tasks. Simplicity can also reduce or eliminate potential problems from human error associated with manual management activities.
But to take this road to simplicity, a tech company needs to start with a core philosophy that provides the discipline to be user-centric, committed to a modern, lean approach, and to navigate the challenges and pitfalls along the way. This is where the architecture of the IT solution gets tested for flexibility and foresight. Nevertheless, the real reason IT solutions get so complex may seem “harmless” at first glance, but it is actually part of a vicious cycle that repeats itself.
Feature Creep Drives Complexity
IT management complexity often comes from what I’ll call “feature creep.” As users become familiar with technology, they see what it can do, and their always-increasing experience also exposes feature gaps and limitations for other features and functionality that they would like.
As new features are then introduced, any features that were not originally planned and expected when a technology was first developed were also never part of any planned management of the overall system. The management of those new features may not only be inconsistent with existing management capabilities but also incompatible with them, requiring independent additional management tools, thereby creating more complexity.
Eventually, new management capabilities are created to simplify or abstract the management of the new features and things get a bit easier — until yet another new feature comes along and it all starts over again.
The Answer To Being Simple Is Simple
The crux of the answer (or antidote) to the “feature creep” is analogous to the doctor’s response in the classic joke about a patient saying, “Doctor, please help me. It hurts when I do this,” to which the doctor replies, “Then stop doing that!”
The key to IT management simplicity is not doing things. Instead, have the system do things for you so that you no longer need to do them manually at all. Unfortunately, over the history of the IT industry, the more common practice has been to constantly try to find ways to make manual management by people easier and easier, such as graphical user interfaces (GUIs) versus command line interfaces (CLIs) and drop-down menu item selection instead of text entry. These things help, but they can never fully solve the bigger problem.
The answer is to use intelligent software to do things automatically as if a really smart person had done them manually. The common overarching term for this, of course, is artificial intelligence (AI). But just as things can change in a system, good software needs to be able to adapt to those changes in real time. That requires a direct subset of AI called machine learning (ML), where the system itself can interpret new information and make a new (good) decision without external human direction.
The ultimate effectiveness can be achieved if a system can employ that rarely seen subset of machine learning known as deep learning (DL). Deep learning is the ability of a system to continuously interpret and evaluate multiple potential options for how to act and then learn from continuously evaluating their relative successes to guide future actions. Developing true deep learning requires much more effort and creativity from really smart people to design it, but the potential effectiveness for the systems and people who will use it is massively greater.
The right approach is to bring the “set it and forget it” mentality to IT management. There are many different areas of IT that can benefit from greater simplicity through intelligent software, such as performance management, capacity planning, predictive maintenance and resource utilization.
But only those companies that “get it” and have implemented technologies that intelligently use software to eliminate the need for extensive human involvement will have the potential to give you those kinds of benefits.
It’s that simple.
